title: Easy exam 11
about: Ten single-choice questions on the basics: startup files, for loops, file ages, here-strings, execute permission, whole-word searches, tar, sessions, signals and filters.

questions.title: Where the aliases live
questions.text: Which file is read by every new interactive shell started in a terminal window, and is the usual place to put your aliases?

options.t: `~/.bashrc`
options.why: It is the per-user file that bash reads when an interactive shell starts.

options.t: `/etc/passwd`
options.why: It lists the accounts of the system; it is not a shell configuration file.

options.t: `~/.bash_history`
options.why: It is where the shell saves the commands you typed, not a place for settings.

options.t: `/etc/shadow`
options.why: It stores password hashes; it has nothing to do with shell startup.

questions.title: for loops
questions.text: Which statement about `for` loops in bash is FALSE?

options.t: `for f in *.txt; do ...; done` runs the body once for each file whose name matches the pattern.
options.why: True: the shell expands the glob before the loop starts.

options.t: `for i in 1 2 3; do ...; done` runs the body three times, with `i` set to 1, 2 and 3.
options.why: True.

options.t: `for i in {1..5}; do ...; done` runs the body five times.
options.why: True: the shell expands the range to `1 2 3 4 5`.

options.t: `for i in $(seq 3); do ...; done` runs the body only once, because `$(seq 3)` is a single word.
options.why: False: the output of `seq 3` is split into the words `1`, `2` and `3`, so the body runs three times.

options.t: `-mtime -1` matches the files modified less than 24 hours ago.
options.why: A minus sign means "less than", counted in periods of 24 hours back from now.

options.t: `-mtime 1` matches the files modified during the last 24 hours.
options.why: A plain `1` means exactly one 24-hour period ago, that is between 24 and 48 hours ago.

options.t: `-mtime +7` matches the files modified exactly seven days ago.
options.why: `+7` means "more than 7" periods, not exactly 7.

options.t: `-mtime` counts calendar days, starting at midnight.
options.why: It counts 24-hour periods back from the moment `find` runs.

questions.title: Text as the input of a command
questions.text: Which command makes `wc -c` read the text `hello` as its standard input, without a file or a pipe?

options.t: `wc -c <<< hello`
options.why: A here-string (`<<<`) feeds the word, followed by a newline, as standard input: it prints `6`.

options.t: `wc -c < hello`
options.why: `<` reads from a file called `hello`, which does not exist: "No such file or directory".

options.t: `wc -c hello`
options.why: `hello` is taken as the name of a file to read, so `wc` reports that it does not exist.

options.t: `wc -c << hello`
options.why: `<<` starts a here-document: the shell waits for lines until it finds one that is just `hello`.

questions.title: Execute for the owner only
questions.text: `script.sh` has mode `rw-r--r--`. Which command gives execute permission to the owner and changes nothing else?

options.t: `chmod u+x script.sh`
options.why: `u+x` adds the execute bit for the user (owner) and leaves every other bit as it was.

options.t: `chmod u=x script.sh`
options.why: `=` sets exactly the listed permissions, so the owner would lose read and write.

options.t: `chmod a+x script.sh`
options.why: It also gives execute permission to the group and to the others.

options.t: `chmod 100 script.sh`
options.why: It sets the mode to `--x------`: the group and the others lose their read permission.

questions.title: Searching for a whole word
questions.text: The file has the lines `a cat sleeps`, `concatenate` and `cat`. Which statement is TRUE?

options.t: `grep -w cat` prints `a cat sleeps` and `cat`, but not `concatenate`.
options.why: `-w` requires the match to be a whole word, with non-word characters (or the line limits) on both sides.

options.t: `grep -w cat` prints all three lines, because every one of them contains `cat`.
options.why: In `concatenate` the letters `cat` are inside a longer word, so `-w` rejects them.

options.t: `grep cat` prints only `cat`, since without options it looks for a whole line.
options.why: Without options `grep` prints every line that contains the pattern anywhere.

options.t: `grep -w cat` prints only the line `cat`, because `-w` means "the whole line".
options.why: The option for matching the whole line is `-x`.

options.t: It packs `docs` into the compressed archive `docs.tgz` and leaves `docs` as it was.
options.why: `c` creates, `z` compresses with gzip and `f` gives the name of the archive.

options.t: It extracts the archive `docs.tgz` into the directory `docs`.
options.why: Extracting needs `x`, not `c`.

options.t: It lists the content of `docs.tgz` without extracting it.
options.why: Listing is done with `t`.

options.t: It compresses each file inside `docs` separately and deletes the originals.
options.why: `tar` packs everything into one archive and does not delete anything; compressing file by file is what `gzip` does.

questions.title: Reading the output of who
questions.text: In the output of `who`, a line shows `pts/0` in the second column. What does that mean?

options.t: A pseudo-terminal: a terminal window or an SSH session.
options.why: `pts/N` are pseudo-terminals; a text console would appear as `ttyN`.

options.t: The user is working on the first text console of the machine.
options.why: A text console is shown as `tty1`, `tty2`...

options.t: The user is working on the graphical display of the machine.
options.why: The graphical display is shown as `:0`.

options.t: The user logged in as `pts` and is the first of the connected users.
options.why: The column shows the terminal the session is attached to, not a user name or an order.

options.t: It sends `SIGKILL`: the process cannot catch or ignore it and ends at once.
options.why: Signal number 9 is `SIGKILL`; the kernel ends the process directly.

options.t: It sends the default signal `SIGTERM`, marked as urgent so that it is delivered before any other.
options.why: `kill` without a number sends `SIGTERM` (15), and signals have no priorities.

options.t: It suspends process 4321 until `kill -18` is sent.
options.why: Suspending is done with `SIGSTOP` (19) or `Ctrl+Z`.

options.t: It sends the signal to the 9 processes that were started last.
options.why: The number is the signal, and the argument is the PID.

questions.title: What is a filter
questions.text: Which statement about filters (commands that read standard input and write standard output) is FALSE?

options.t: `sort`, `tr` and `wc` can be used as filters in a pipeline.
options.why: True: with no file argument they read their standard input.

options.t: `grep pattern` with no file name reads standard input.
options.why: True: that is why it works at the end of a pipe.

options.t: `cat` with no arguments copies its standard input to its standard output.
options.why: True.

options.t: `ls` is a filter: it reads a list of names from its standard input and prints them.
options.why: False: `ls` ignores its input and lists the current directory (or the arguments), so `echo /tmp | ls` does not list `/tmp`.
